title: Arguments for God: the first cause
examples: What is the first cause argument?
If everything has a cause, what caused God?

explain.say: Think of a row of dominoes falling. Each one is knocked over by the one before it. But something must have pushed the first one. The first cause argument says the universe is like that.

Here is the argument step by step. Everything that begins has a cause. The chain of causes cannot go back forever. So there must be a first cause that was not itself caused, and believers call this first cause God.

items: Everything that begins has a cause
The chain cannot go back forever
So there is a first, uncaused cause

explain.say: The most famous version comes from Thomas Aquinas, a Christian thinker of the 1200s. Three of his Five Ways argue from motion, from causes, and from things that might not have existed, building on the ancient Greek philosopher Aristotle.

items: First way | Things move and change | An unmoved mover
Second way | Things are caused | An uncaused first cause
Third way | Things might not have existed | A necessary being

draw.text: The Muslim thinker al-Ghazali gave a version called the kalam argument: the universe began, so it has a cause.

explain.say: Critics raise strong objections. If everything needs a cause, what caused God? Why couldn't the universe itself just exist, or the chain go back forever? And even if there is a first cause, why must it be a loving God?

items: Maybe the universe itself needs no cause
Maybe the chain goes back forever
A first cause need not be a personal, loving God

draw.text: David Hume and Bertrand Russell pressed these points.

explain.say: Believers reply that the argument does not say everything needs a cause, only things that begin or could have failed to exist. God, they say, is eternal and necessary, so God needs no cause. The debate turns on whether that reply works.

b: Only things that begin need a cause

explain.say: Underneath it all is a question the philosopher Leibniz asked, and it still puzzles believers and non-believers alike: why is there something rather than nothing?

draw.value: Why is there something rather than nothing?
draw.label: Leibniz

faq.q: What is the first cause argument?
faq.a: The first cause argument says that everything that begins has a cause, and the chain of causes cannot go back forever, so there must be a first cause that was not caused by anything else. Believers say this first cause is God. It is also called the cosmological argument.

faq.q: If everything has a cause, what caused God?
faq.a: This is the most famous objection. Believers reply that the argument does not claim everything has a cause, only things that begin to exist or might not have existed. They hold that God is eternal and necessary, so needs no cause. Critics answer that if something can be uncaused, perhaps the universe itself could be.

Thomas Aquinas, in the 1200s, gave five short arguments for God: from motion, to an unmoved mover; from causes, to a first cause; from contingency, to a necessary being; from degrees of goodness, to a highest good; and from order in nature, to a designer. The first three are forms of the cosmological argument.

The unmoved mover is an idea from Aristotle, taken up by Aquinas. Everything that changes is changed by something else, so there must be a first source of all change that is not itself changed by anything. Aquinas identified this with God.

The kalam argument comes from Islamic philosophy, especially al-Ghazali in the 11th century, and was revived by the modern philosopher William Lane Craig. It runs: whatever begins to exist has a cause; the universe began to exist; so the universe has a cause.

faq.q: Does the Big Bang prove the first cause argument?
faq.a: Some believers say the Big Bang supports it, because it suggests the universe had a beginning. Others point out that physicists do not yet know what, if anything, came before the Big Bang, and that a beginning of the universe would not by itself show what caused it.
asks: did God cause the Big Bang

faq.q: What did Hume say about the first cause?
faq.a: David Hume, an 18th-century Scottish philosopher, argued that we only learn about causes by seeing things happen inside the universe, so we cannot be sure the universe as a whole needs a cause. He also asked why the chain of causes could not simply go back forever.
asks: Hume's objection to the cosmological argument

faq.q: What did Bertrand Russell say about the first cause?
faq.a: In a 1948 radio debate with the priest Frederick Copleston, Bertrand Russell said the universe might just be there, and that is all. He also argued it is a mistake to move from every human having a mother to the whole human race having a mother.

faq.q: Why can't the chain of causes go back forever?
faq.a: Supporters say an endless chain would never explain why there is any chain at all, like a train of carriages with no engine. Critics reply that mathematics handles infinities easily, and that each link in an endless chain could still be explained by the one before it.

faq.q: Does the first cause have to be God?
faq.a: That is a key weakness critics point out. Even if there is a first cause, the argument alone does not show it is personal, all-powerful, loving or the God of any particular religion. Believers often combine it with other arguments and with faith to fill in that picture.
asks: could the first cause be something else
is the first cause the God of the Bible
why call the first cause God

faq.q: Do other religions have a first cause idea?
faq.a: Many traditions ask where everything comes from. Some Hindu thinkers describe Brahman as the source and ground of all things. Buddhism, by contrast, generally does not focus on a creator or a first beginning, and Jainism teaches that the universe has always existed without a creator.
asks: do Buddhists believe in a first cause

faq.q: Does the first cause argument prove God exists?
faq.a: Philosophers still disagree. Supporters find it a powerful reason to believe there is an ultimate cause of everything; critics think its steps can be questioned. Whether it convinces you depends on how you weigh the steps and the objections.
asks: is the first cause argument true

faq.q: Why is there something rather than nothing?
faq.a: That question, asked by the philosopher Leibniz, is at the heart of the first cause argument. Leibniz answered that there must be a sufficient reason for everything, ultimately God. Others think the universe may simply exist without a further explanation, or that science may one day say more.

facts: The first cause argument is also called the cosmological argument.
Thomas Aquinas set out his Five Ways in the Summa Theologiae in the 13th century.
The idea of an unmoved mover comes from the ancient Greek philosopher Aristotle.
The kalam argument was developed in Islamic philosophy, notably by al-Ghazali in the 11th century.
Bertrand Russell and Frederick Copleston debated the first cause argument on BBC radio in 1948.

quiz.why: Thomas Aquinas set out the Five Ways in the 13th century; the first three are cosmological arguments.

wrong.1: Paley is known for the design argument and the watchmaker.

options.say: God was caused by the universe
